sections.name: MCQ Set A
tips: Read the question stem before the source so you know what you are looking for.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the idea the source shows (cause, effect, continuity, change, connection between regions), then pick the option that matches that idea.
Eliminate options that are true in history but not shown by the source, or that belong to the wrong time or region.
Watch for extreme words ("only," "all," "first," "created," "ended," "every"): they are usually wrong.
For "claim" or "evidence the author uses" questions, the answer must be stated or directly supported in the text. Do not use outside knowledge to pick it.
For point-of-view questions, ask who wrote it, when, for whom, and why.

S1.title: Mansa Musa of Mali in Cairo, 1324
S1.attr: Adapted from an Arabic account written about a decade later.
S1.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S1.text: The king of Mali, Musa, entered Cairo on his way to Mecca with a very large retinue. He and his companions spent and gave away so much gold to officials and to the poor of the city that its value in the markets fell sharply. Merchants who dealt in gold had not recovered their losses twelve years later. The king told his hosts that his kingdom lay many months' journey to the south, beyond the great desert, and that he meant to bring learned men home with him.

S2.title: The Mongols: Destroyers and Connectors
S2.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S2.text: The Mongols are remembered for slaughter, and the memory is deserved: Baghdad was sacked in 1258 and much of its population killed. Yet the same conquerors made the long overland routes safer than they had been in centuries. Roads were repaired and bandits were punished wherever Mongol authority reached, and a relay system of messengers and stations linked distant provinces. Merchants who had once paid tolls to a dozen rival rulers now dealt with a single authority that respected trade. It is no accident that the travelers who carried medical learning, numbers, and technology between Asia and Europe moved in these decades.

S3.title: A Persian envoy describes Calicut, 1442
S3.attr: Abdu Razzak, Persian envoy who visited the port of Calicut, in his description of the city, 1442.
S3.text: Wealthy merchants bring in big cargoes, which they unload and unhesitatingly send into the markets without thinking in the meantime of any security, or checking the account, or keeping watch over the goods.

S4.title: A Moroccan scholar sets out, 1325
S4.attr: Ibn Battuta, a Muslim scholar from Morocco, describing his departure at age 21, from the account of his travels dictated years later.
S4.text: I set out alone, having neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer, nor caravan whose part I might join, but swayed by an overmastering impulse within me and a desire long-cherished in my bosom to visit these illustrious sanctuaries.

S5.title: The plague arrives in a port city, 1347
S5.attr: Adapted from a fourteenth-century European chronicle.
S5.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: Merchants returning from the Black Sea ports in the autumn of 1347 brought with them a sickness that struck the harbor quarter first. Within weeks the dead lay in the streets, and physicians trained in the learning of the Arabs and the Greeks were unable to cure it.

By the next harvest, many villages stood empty. Landowners who had once dictated terms to their tenants now begged laborers to work their fields, and the workers who survived demanded wages that would have been unthinkable a few years earlier. Some lords complained that the world had been turned upside down.

questions.stem: The author most likely mentions that gold merchants had not recovered their losses twelve years later in order to
options: criticize Musa for wasting Mali's wealth on a pilgrimage.
show that Cairo's gold merchants knew little about West Africa.
show how a ruler's wealth could reshape distant economies.
explain why Mali's gold supply was soon exhausted.
questions.exp: The twelve-year effect shows that one ruler's spending reshaped prices in a distant economy. The author reports the loss without criticizing Musa, says nothing about what Cairo's merchants knew of West Africa, and never suggests that Mali's gold ran out.
why: The author only reports the effect on Cairo's gold market. Nothing in the detail criticizes Musa or calls his spending wasteful.
The detail is about how long the losses lasted, not about what Cairo's merchants knew of West Africa.
The passage never says Mali's gold ran out; the loss was in Cairo's market, not in Mali's supply.

questions.stem: The effect on Cairo's gold market described in the passage best illustrates which of the following about trade networks in this period?
options: Distant regions were economically linked, so events in one could affect prices in another.
West African gold was valued more highly in Egypt than in any other region of Africa or Asia.
Muslim pilgrims in Cairo carried goods for sale between Mecca and North Africa.
Rulers used gifts of gold to secure the loyalty of officials in other states.
questions.exp: The effect on Cairo's prices shows that distant regions were economically linked. The passage does not say gold was valued more in Egypt than elsewhere, describe pilgrims selling goods, or say the gifts were meant to buy loyalty.
why: The passage never compares Egypt's valuation of gold with other regions; it only shows the effect on Cairo's prices.
No pilgrims selling goods between Mecca and North Africa are described in the passage.
Musa's gifts are not described as buying officials' loyalty; this answer adds a motive the source does not give.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how a ruler from beyond the great desert could reach Cairo, despite the distance described in the passage?
options: Mongol authority over North Africa had made desert travel safe for pilgrims.
Sea routes along the Atlantic coast carried most pilgrims from West Africa to Egypt.
Cairo's rulers sent armies each year to escort pilgrims across the Sahara.
Camel caravans moving between oases already linked West Africa and North Africa.
questions.exp: Camel caravans moving between desert oases already linked West Africa with North Africa, and Musa's journey used those links. The Mongols did not rule the Sahara, Atlantic sea routes were not how pilgrims reached Egypt, and nothing describes Cairo sending escorts.
why: The Mongols did not rule North Africa or the Sahara, so their authority cannot explain Musa's journey.
Pilgrims from West Africa reached Egypt over desert routes, not by sea along the Atlantic coast.
Nothing in the passage says Cairo sent armies to escort pilgrims; this is invented.

questions.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence does the author use most directly to support the claim that Mongol rule benefited merchants?
options: Baghdad was sacked in 1258 and much of its population was killed.
Medical learning, numbers, and technology were carried between Asia and Europe by travelers.
Merchants dealt with a single authority instead of paying tolls to many rulers.
A relay system of messengers and stations linked the distant provinces.
questions.exp: The author says merchants who once paid tolls to a dozen rulers now dealt with one authority that respected trade; that is the evidence aimed directly at merchants. The sack of Baghdad supports the destruction claim, and the relay system and the movement of learning are about communication and ideas, not merchants' costs.
why: The sack of Baghdad supports the claim that the Mongols were destructive, not that they benefited merchants.
This is evidence about the spread of ideas and technology, not about the cost or safety of trade for merchants.
The relay system is evidence about communication between provinces, not about what merchants paid or risked.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the author cite as evidence that the routes were safer under the Mongols than in previous centuries?
options: Travelers carried medical learning, numbers, and technology between Asia and Europe.
Roads were repaired and bandits were punished wherever Mongol authority reached.
Merchants had previously paid tolls to as many as a dozen rival rulers.
Baghdad's fall in 1258 removed a rival power from the trade routes.
questions.exp: Repaired roads and punished bandits are the author's direct evidence of safety. The toll detail describes the earlier cost of trade, not safety; the movement of learning is a result, and the passage does not link Baghdad's fall to safer routes.
why: The movement of learning and technology is a result of connection, not evidence that routes were safer.
The tolls describe what trade cost before the Mongols, not whether travel was safe.
The passage does not link Baghdad's fall to safer routes; this is an unsupported connection.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's overall argument about the Mongol Empire?
options: Mongol violence was exaggerated by later writers, and its effects on trade were minor.
Mongol rule benefited merchants only because the empire deliberately promoted cultural exchange across Eurasia.
The Mongols destroyed existing trade routes and then rebuilt them to serve their own armies.
Mongol conquest was destructive, yet it created conditions that encouraged exchange across Eurasia.
questions.exp: The author says the reputation for slaughter is deserved and that Mongol authority also made routes safer and encouraged exchange. The words "exaggerated," "only," and "to serve their own armies" claim more than the passage says.
why: The author says the Mongols' reputation for slaughter is deserved, so violence was not exaggerated.
The word 'only' and the claim that the Mongols deliberately promoted cultural exchange go beyond the passage.
The passage does not say the Mongols destroyed the routes and rebuilt them for their armies.

questions.stem: The conduct of the merchants described in the passage can best be used as evidence of
options: the role of stable, well-governed ports in long-distance trade.
the growing use of credit instruments by Indian Ocean merchants.
the importance of Muslim merchants in Indian Ocean commerce.
the dominance of Indian merchants over East African trade.
questions.exp: Merchants who leave valuable cargo unwatched must trust that the port is secure, which shows how stable states supported trade. The passage says nothing about credit instruments, the role of Muslim merchants, or Indian dominance over East African trade.
why: Credit instruments are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
The passage does not focus on the role of Muslim merchants; it is about merchants trusting the port.
The passage says nothing about Indian merchants dominating East African trade.

questions.skill: Evaluating what would challenge an inference
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would make the merchants' conduct described in the passage most difficult to explain?
options: Merchants trading in Calicut came from many different regions of Asia and Africa.
Most goods reaching Calicut arrived by sea rather than by overland caravan.
Calicut's rulers had no means of keeping order in the city's markets.
The envoy who wrote the account was a Muslim from Central Asia.
questions.exp: The merchants' trust in unguarded cargo makes sense only if the port was secure, so rulers who could not keep order would contradict it. Where the merchants came from, how goods arrived, and the envoy's origin do not affect whether the port was safe.
why: Merchants coming from many regions fits a busy port and does not contradict their trust in its security.
Whether goods arrive by sea or by caravan does not affect whether merchants can trust the port.
The envoy's origin does not change how safe the port was.

questions.stem: Merchants trading at Calicut in 1442 most clearly illustrate which of the following continuities?
options: The dominance of overland caravans in moving luxury goods between Asia and the Middle East.
Indian Ocean commerce, which had thrived long before the Mongols or the Ming voyages.
The reliance of Indian Ocean traders on Chinese state fleets for protection.
The control of Indian Ocean ports by a single empire that unified the region.
questions.exp: Indian Ocean trade existed as early as 200 B.C.E. and continued and grew in this period. The source shows a busy port, not overland caravans, Chinese protection, or one unifying empire.
why: The passage shows a sea port, not overland caravans moving luxury goods.
The merchants are not shown relying on Chinese fleets for protection.
The source shows a busy port, not one empire controlling the whole Indian Ocean.

questions.stem: The passage most clearly reflects which of the following motives for travel in this period?
options: A merchant's wish to profit from trade in luxury goods.
A diplomat's duty to deliver a ruler's message abroad.
A refugee's wish to escape the turmoil of Mongol conquests.
A traveler's religious devotion to holy places.
questions.exp: The author says an overmastering impulse and a long-cherished desire drove him to visit illustrious sanctuaries, which shows religious devotion as a motive. He never mentions profit, a diplomatic duty, or fleeing turmoil.
why: The author never mentions profit or trade as his reason for leaving.
The author is not delivering a ruler's message; he leaves for personal reasons.
He does not mention Mongol conquests or fleeing turmoil.

questions.stem: A historian using this passage as evidence of why people traveled in this period should most carefully consider that
options: it reflects one Muslim scholar's religious motives, which may not represent merchants' motives.
it was dictated to a scribe years later, which makes every detail in it unreliable for historians studying the period.
it describes a solitary departure, so it cannot be connected to any trade network.
it was composed in Arabic, so it cannot reflect experiences beyond Muslim-ruled lands.
questions.exp: Ibn Battuta wrote as a devout Muslim scholar traveling to holy places, so his motives may differ from a merchant's. The other options overstate: later dictation does not make every detail unreliable, one traveler can still use trade networks, and language does not limit where an author traveled.
why: Later dictation can reduce accuracy, but it does not make every detail unreliable; 'every' is too extreme.
One traveler's departure can still use trade networks; the passage does not prove it was cut off from them.
The language of a text does not limit where its author traveled.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: The sickness reached the Black Sea ports before spreading to the harbor quarter.
Physicians trained in Arab and Greek learning were unable to cure the sickness.
Merchants from the Black Sea ports deliberately spread the sickness through the city.
Most of the city's physicians died before the sickness reached the streets.
questions.exp: The paragraph says the physicians could not cure it. It says merchants brought the sickness, not that they spread it deliberately, and it does not say the physicians died first.
why: The paragraph does not say the sickness reached the Black Sea ports before the harbor quarter.
The merchants brought the sickness, but nothing says they spread it deliberately.
The paragraph does not say the physicians died before the sickness reached the streets.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a claim made in the second paragraph?
options: Lords forced the surviving laborers to stay on their land at the old wages.
Villages emptied because lords had moved their tenants into the larger cities.
Surviving workers demanded higher wages, and landowners had to beg for labor.
Lords blamed a decline in religious belief for turning the world upside down.
questions.exp: The paragraph says landowners begged laborers to work and workers demanded much higher wages. It does not say lords forced workers to stay, moved tenants to cities, or blamed religion.
why: The paragraph says workers demanded higher wages; it does not say lords forced them to stay at old wages.
Villages emptied because of the plague, not because lords moved tenants into cities.
Lords are not said to have blamed a decline in religious belief.

S6.title: Ibn Battuta in Mali, c. 1352
S6.attr: Ibn Battuta, a Muslim scholar from Morocco, describing his travels along the Niger River and across the Sahara.
S6.text: From Timbuktu I sailed down the Nile [Niger] on a small boat, hollowed out of a single piece of wood...I went on . . . to Gawgaw [Gao], which is a large city on the Nile [Niger]... The buying and selling of its inhabitants is done with cowry-shells, and the same is the case at Malli [the city of Mali]. I stayed there about a month, and then set out in the direction of Tagadda by land with a large caravan of merchants from Ghadamas.

S7.title: Old Tools, Bigger Scale
S7.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S7.text: Historians sometimes credit the Mongols with inventing the commercial tools of the Silk Roads, but the tools were older. Caravanserai, roadside inns where travelers could rest and trade animals, had already been built in Persia centuries earlier. The Chinese had long used money, and their government had developed flying cash, a form of credit that let merchants deposit paper money in one city and collect it in another. What changed after 1200 was scale: under a single Mongol authority, these tools served many more merchants over far greater distances, and banking houses in European cities adopted similar practices in the 1300s.

S8.title: Towns of the Zanj coast
S8.attr: Adapted from a medieval geographer's description of the East African coast.
S8.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S8.text: The towns of the Zanj coast are built of coral stone and are governed by their own rulers. Their merchants buy ivory, gold, and enslaved people from the interior and sell them to ships that arrive with the monsoon from Arabia, Persia, and India. Porcelain from China is common in their houses. The people speak a language of the coast that contains many Arabic words, and most of the leading men are Muslims.

S9.title: The plague in Florence
S9.attr: Giovanni Boccaccio, an Italian author who lived through the plague in Florence, writing around 1350.

S10.title: Champa rice in China
S10.attr: Adapted summary of a historian's account.
S10.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: The Chinese court received Champa rice from the rulers of Champa as tribute. The rice ripened quickly and resisted both drought and flood, and in good years a farmer could harvest two crops from the same field.

As rice farming spread across the southern lowlands and up terraced hillsides, the population grew and many families moved southward. Cities in the south expanded, and merchants found new buyers for their goods.

questions.stem: The use of cowrie shells described in the passage is best used as evidence of
options: the spread of Chinese paper money into the Niger valley.
the control of Niger valley markets by North African merchants.
regional differences in the money used by trading networks.
the replacement of coins by credit across the Islamic world.
questions.exp: Different networks used different forms of money: West African states used cowrie shells, while China used flying cash and paper money and other regions used metal coins. The passage says nothing about paper money in the Niger valley, control by North African merchants, or credit replacing coins.
why: Nothing in the passage mentions Chinese paper money in the Niger valley.
The cowrie shells show local currency, not control of markets by North African merchants.
The passage does not say credit replaced coins; cowrie shells are a physical currency.

questions.skill: Connecting a source to a feature of a network
questions.stem: Ibn Battuta's departure from Mali with a large caravan of merchants most directly reflects which feature of trans-Saharan trade?
options: Its reliance on organized caravans to cross the desert in groups.
Its dependence on seasonal winds to time long voyages across the Indian Ocean.
Its protection by a single empire that stretched across Persia and China.
Its use of roadside inns that sheltered travelers along the Silk Roads.
questions.exp: Merchants crossed the Sahara in organized caravans for safety and supplies. Monsoon timing belongs to the Indian Ocean, a single empire from Persia to China describes the Mongols, and roadside inns were a Silk Road feature.
why: Seasonal winds belong to Indian Ocean sailing, not to desert caravans.
A single empire stretching from Persia to China describes the Mongols, not trans-Saharan trade.
Roadside inns (caravanserai) were a Silk Road feature, not a trans-Saharan one.

questions.skill: Drawing a conclusion from a source
questions.stem: That Ibn Battuta could join a caravan of merchants from Ghadames after visiting Mali best supports which conclusion about West Africa in the 14th century?
options: West African rulers relied on Mongol protection for their trade routes.
Muslim merchants had replaced local merchants in the Niger valley cities.
West African states had abandoned local currencies for Muslim coins.
West African cities were linked to trade networks across the Sahara.
questions.exp: Joining a caravan from North Africa shows that Mali's cities were tied into trans-Saharan trade. The Mongols did not rule West Africa, nothing shows local merchants were replaced, and the same passage says cowrie shells, a local currency, were still in use.
why: The Mongols did not rule West Africa or protect its routes.
Joining a caravan does not show local merchants were replaced.
The same passage says cowrie shells, a local currency, were still used.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the author use as evidence that the commercial tools of the Silk Roads were older than the Mongol Empire?
options: Under one authority the tools served far more merchants over greater distances.
Caravanserai had already been built in Persia centuries before the Mongols.
European banking houses adopted similar practices in the 1300s.
Mongol rulers preferred paper money to coins for all government payments.
questions.exp: The author points to caravanserai built in Persia centuries earlier as proof the tools were older. The increase in scale and the European banking houses describe what happened after 1200, and the passage says nothing about Mongol preferences for paper money.
why: Greater scale after the Mongols is evidence of change, not that the tools were older.
European banking houses adopting practices in the 1300s comes after 1200 and does not show the tools were older.
The passage says nothing about Mongol rulers preferring paper money.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the commercial tools were older than the Mongol Empire?
options: Banking houses in European cities copied practices that were first used in China.
Records show that merchants used these tools far more often under Mongol rule than before.
Chinese sources show that paper money was already in use before the Mongol conquests.
Excavations show the earliest caravanserai in Persia date from after the Mongols.
questions.exp: The argument depends on the tools existing before the Mongols. Evidence that the earliest caravanserai were built after the Mongol conquests would undercut it, while European copying, greater use under Mongol rule, and earlier Chinese paper money are all consistent with the author's claims.
why: European copying of earlier Chinese practices is consistent with the claim and does not weaken it.
More use under Mongol rule is consistent with tools that were older but used more widely.
Paper money already in use before the Mongols would support, not weaken, the claim.

questions.stem: The author's argument is best described as an example of which of the following types of historical reasoning?
options: Continuity and change, since the tools were older but their scale grew.
Comparison, since the author sets two networks of exchange side by side.
Causation, since the author traces one single event to one outcome.
Periodization, since the author splits history at the Mongol conquests.
questions.exp: The author argues that the tools were older (continuity) but that their scale grew after 1200 (change). The passage does not compare two networks, trace one event to one outcome, or divide history at the Mongol conquests.
why: The author is not setting two networks side by side; the argument is about one set of tools over time.
The passage does not trace one event to one outcome.
The author does not divide history at the Mongol conquests; the tools exist on both sides of it.

questions.stem: The language described in the passage best illustrates which of the following?
options: The conquest of the entire East African coast by large organized Arab armies.
The spread of Chinese writing along Indian Ocean trade routes.
Cultural blending produced by contact between merchants and coastal peoples.
The decline of Bantu-speaking societies once Islam had arrived.
questions.exp: The Swahili language blends Bantu and Arabic, reflecting Arab and Persian merchants mixing with local peoples in diasporic communities. The passage mentions no conquest, Chinese writing, or decline of Bantu-speaking societies.
why: No conquest by Arab armies is mentioned; the language reflects mixing through trade.
The passage does not mention Chinese writing; the language blends Bantu and Arabic.
Swahili shows Bantu languages blending with Arabic, not Bantu societies declining.

questions.stem: The phrase "with the monsoon" in the passage best illustrates the importance of which of the following to Indian Ocean trade?
options: Control of narrow straits by powerful and well-funded state navies.
Seasonal winds that decided when voyages could be made.
Protection of coastal ports by walls and garrisons.
Large state fleets that carried tribute to rulers.
questions.exp: Ships that arrive with the monsoon show that seasonal winds determined when Indian Ocean voyages could be made. The passage does not mention navies, fortifications, or state fleets.
why: The phrase is about winds, not about navies controlling straits.
Walls and garrisons are not mentioned; the monsoon is a natural feature.
State fleets carrying tribute are not what 'with the monsoon' describes.

questions.stem: The passage is best used as evidence for which of the following arguments about Indian Ocean trade?
options: Mongol rule protected Indian Ocean shipping lanes from Persia to East Africa.
Chinese fleets dominated the ports of the East African coast.
Islam spread along the East African coast through military conquest.
Trade linked East African towns to producers and buyers across the ocean.
questions.exp: Ivory and gold sold to ships from Arabia, Persia, and India, and Chinese porcelain in local houses, show East Africa tied into a wide network of exchange. The passage does not mention Mongol protection, Chinese naval dominance, or conquest as the way Islam arrived.
why: The Mongols did not rule the Indian Ocean; the passage does not mention Mongol protection.
Chinese porcelain in houses shows trade, not that Chinese fleets dominated the ports.
The passage does not say Islam spread by conquest; it describes trade.

questions.stem: For which of the following historical questions would this quotation be most useful?
options: How people experienced the plague in a European city.
Why the plague began in Central Asia before reaching Europe.
How many people died from the plague across Eurasia.
Which trade routes carried the plague from Asia to Europe.
questions.exp: A single vivid line from a witness shows how people experienced the plague. It gives no information about where the disease began, how many people died, or which routes carried it.
why: A single quotation about the plague in Florence cannot explain where the plague began.
One witness line cannot give the death toll across Eurasia.
The quotation does not mention trade routes.

questions.stem: A historian using this quotation to study the plague's effects on European society should most carefully consider that
options: it was written after the plague ended, so it cannot describe conditions accurately for historians.
it describes Florence alone, so it cannot say anything about the plague elsewhere.
it reflects one educated Italian's view of one city, not rural or non-European areas.
it was written in Italian, so it cannot be compared with Asian accounts.
questions.exp: Boccaccio was an educated Italian describing Florence, so his account may not represent rural villages or other regions. The other options overstate: being written after the plague or about one city does not make an account useless, and language does not prevent comparison.
why: Being written after the plague does not make an account inaccurate; the answer is too extreme.
An account of one city can still say something about the plague, so 'cannot say anything' is too extreme.
Language does not prevent comparison with Asian accounts; the answer overstates.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: Chinese farmers developed Champa rice to resist drought and flood.
Farmers could sometimes harvest two crops from the same field.
The rulers of Champa bought the rice from Chinese merchants.
Champa rice replaced all other rice grown in southern China.
questions.exp: The paragraph says a farmer could sometimes harvest two crops from the same field. It says the rice reached China as tribute from Champa, not that Chinese farmers developed it or that Champa bought it, and it does not say Champa rice replaced all other rice.
why: The paragraph says the rice came to China as tribute from Champa; it does not say Chinese farmers developed it.
The rice reached China as tribute from Champa, not by Champa buying it from Chinese merchants.
The paragraph does not say Champa rice replaced all other rice; 'all' is too strong.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a claim made in the second paragraph?
options: Rice farming spread, the population grew, and many families moved south.
Merchants forced farmers to plant rice so that cities could be fed.
Terraced hillsides were abandoned once the lowlands had filled with farmers.
Population growth was fastest in northern cities where wheat was grown.
questions.exp: The paragraph links the spread of rice farming with population growth, southward movement, expanding cities, and new buyers for merchants. The other options invent merchant coercion, abandoned terraces, or northern wheat growth.
why: The paragraph does not say merchants forced farmers to plant rice.
No abandonment of terraced hillsides is mentioned.
Northern wheat-growing cities are not part of the paragraph's claim.

S16.title: Angkor Thom
S16.attr: Adapted from a textbook description of the royal monuments of the Khmer Empire.
S16.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S16.text: The Khmer Empire, in present-day Cambodia, was the most successful kingdom in Southeast Asia. The royal monuments at Angkor Thom show both Hindu and Buddhist influences. Hindu artwork and sculptures of Hindu gods adorned the city. Later, when Khmer rulers had become Buddhist, they added Buddhist sculptures and artwork onto buildings while keeping the Hindu artwork.

S17.title: Cultural influences of Islam in Afro-Eurasia
S17.label: Practice source (adapted for practice).
table: The Swahili language blends Bantu and Arabic; Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning; leaders deepened Islamic ties through pilgrimages to Mecca
Islam's emphasis on equality attracted lower-caste Hindus; architecture blended Hindu designs with Islamic patterns; the Urdu language drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian
Javanese stories, puppetry, and poetry absorbed Muslim characters and techniques

S18.title: Women in the Mongol Empire
S18.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S18.text: In the Mongols' nomadic culture, women tended flocks of sheep and goats in addition to raising children and providing meals. Because they rode horses as men did, Mongol women wore the same kind of leather trousers. They could remarry after being widowed and could start divorces. In the lands the Mongols ruled, Mongol women moved about freely, and women were often top advisors to the great khan.

S19.title: The kingdom of Gujarat
S19.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S19.text: The western Indian kingdom of Gujarat became the go-between for trade between the East and West. Its rulers raised money through customs, which were taxes on imported goods, and through fees for the use of seaports. The revenue from customs in Gujarat was many times greater than the entire worth of some European states.

S20.title: Learning and technology on the trade routes
S20.attr: Adapted summary of a textbook account.
S20.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: Islamic scholars translated Greek literary classics into Arabic, saving the works of Aristotle and other thinkers. They also brought back mathematics texts from India and techniques for making paper from China.
Papermaking reached Europe from China in the 13th century. Together with printing technology, it helped lead to a rise in literacy.

questions.stem: The monuments described in the passage best illustrate which of the following about the spread of Indian religions into Southeast Asia?
options: Buddhism completely replaced Hinduism once Khmer rulers converted.
Indian religions spread mainly when Indian armies conquered Southeast Asia.
Southeast Asian rulers rejected Indian religious influence in their architecture.
New religions were often added to earlier traditions rather than replacing them.
questions.exp: The Khmer rulers added Buddhist art while keeping the Hindu art, which shows that religions often blended or coexisted rather than replacing one another. Indian religions spread through trade, not conquest by Indian armies, and the monuments show acceptance of Indian influence, not rejection.
why: The monuments show Buddhist art added alongside Hindu art, not one replacing the other.
Indian religions spread through trade and contact, not conquest by Indian armies.
The Khmer rulers built Indian-influenced monuments, so they accepted rather than rejected Indian influence.

questions.stem: Which additional evidence would best support the claim that Khmer rulers used religion to strengthen their authority?
options: Merchants from India described the temples in letters sent home.
Sculptures showed kings sharing the powers of Hindu gods.
Farmers paid taxes in rice to support the builders of the city.
Buddhist monks lived in monasteries on the edges of the capital.
questions.exp: Showing kings as sharing divine powers directly links religion to royal authority, as in Khmer ideas of divine kingship. Travelers' letters, tax payments, and monks living nearby do not show religion being used to support rule.
why: Merchants' letters about the temples do not show rulers using religion to support their authority.
Farmers paying taxes in rice supports the builders but does not link religion to royal authority.
Monks living near the capital does not show rulers using religion to strengthen their rule.

questions.skill: Drawing an inference from a source
questions.stem: Which of the following can best be inferred about the role of religious imagery on the royal monuments?
options: It helped rulers collect customs duties from foreign merchants.
It showed that rulers wished to end earlier religious traditions.
Royal monuments linked the ruling family with divine imagery.
It was designed mainly to attract Chinese merchants to Cambodia.
questions.exp: Monuments built by rulers and filled with religious art tied the royal family to sacred authority; Khmer kings drew on Hindu ideas of divine kingship. Nothing in the passage connects the imagery to customs duties, ending older traditions, or attracting Chinese merchants.
why: Nothing links the religious imagery to customs duties.
The monuments kept older traditions alongside new ones, so rulers did not want to end them.
Attracting Chinese merchants is not mentioned as the purpose of the imagery.

questions.skill: Drawing a conclusion from a source
questions.stem: Which of the following is best supported by the information in the table?
options: The spread of Islam produced blended cultures rather than uniform ones.
Islam spread primarily through military conquest in each of the three regions listed.
Islamic learning remained limited to cities in sub-Saharan Africa.
Local traditions disappeared once Islam arrived in each region.
questions.exp: The Swahili language, blended architecture, Urdu, and Javanese puppetry with Muslim characters all show cultural blending. The table does not mention conquest, does not limit Islamic learning to Africa, and does not say local traditions disappeared.
why: The table does not say Islam spread mainly through conquest in all three regions.
The table does not say Islamic learning was limited to cities in sub-Saharan Africa.
The table shows local traditions blending with Islam, not disappearing.

questions.stem: A student claims Islam spread in South Asia mainly through force. Which detail in the table most directly challenges that claim?
options: Architecture blended Hindu designs with Islamic patterns.
Leaders in Africa deepened Islamic ties through pilgrimages to Mecca.
The Urdu language drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian.
Islam's emphasis on equality attracted lower-caste Hindus.
questions.exp: Lower-caste Hindus being attracted by Islam's emphasis on equality points to voluntary conversion for social reasons, which challenges the claim of force. The architecture and Urdu show blending, and the pilgrimage detail concerns Africa, not South Asia.
why: Blended architecture shows cultural mixing but does not address whether conversion was forced.
The pilgrimage detail concerns Africa, not South Asia.
Urdu shows blending but says nothing about whether Islam spread by force.

questions.stem: The existence of the Urdu language best illustrates
options: the replacement of Persian by Arabic across South Asia.
Mongol efforts to unify their empire under one script.
cultural blending that followed Islam's arrival in South Asia.
the isolation of South Asian languages from outside influence.
questions.exp: Urdu drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian, which shows blending after Islam arrived. Uyghur script, not Urdu, was the Mongol writing system, and Urdu neither replaced Persian nor shows isolation.
why: Urdu drew on Persian as well as Arabic; it did not show Persian being replaced.
The Mongol script was Uyghur, not Urdu.
Urdu drew on Hindi, Arabic, and Persian, so it shows outside influence, not isolation.

questions.stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following about gender in Afro-Eurasia in this period?
options: Women gained equal political power in nearly every society of the period.
Women's roles varied, and some enjoyed more freedom than was typical.
Nomadic societies gave women fewer rights than farming societies did.
Patriarchal norms vanished in every society the Mongols conquered.
questions.exp: Mongol women had more freedom than women in most other parts of Afro-Eurasia, even though the empire was still a patriarchy. The passage does not support equal power everywhere, fewer rights for nomadic women, or the disappearance of patriarchy.
why: 'Equal political power in nearly every society' is much stronger than the passage supports.
The passage says Mongol women had more freedom, not fewer rights.
The empire was still a patriarchy; norms did not vanish.

questions.stem: The roles of Mongol women are best used to illustrate which of the following about the relationship between environment and society?
options: A way of life shaped by environment could produce different gender roles.
Religious teachings were the main source of gender norms in every society.
Wealth from conquest was the main reason women gained greater freedom.
Patriarchal norms were weaker wherever long-distance trade was heavy.
questions.exp: Herding and horse-riding on the steppe gave women practical roles that differed from those in settled societies, which shows how environment and way of life shaped gender roles. The other options rely on extreme or unsupported claims such as 'in every society' and 'wherever trade was heavy.'
why: 'Main source in every society' is an extreme claim the passage does not make.
Wealth from conquest is not given as the reason women had freedom.
'Wherever long-distance trade was heavy' is unsupported by the passage.

questions.stem: The freedoms of Mongol women are best used as evidence of which of the following?
options: Social structures were identical in every single part of the Mongol Empire.
Mongol rule ended class distinctions among the people it conquered.
The Mongol Empire was the only patriarchal society in Afro-Eurasia.
Gender norms differed even among societies that were mostly patriarchal.
questions.exp: Societies were mostly patriarchal, yet Mongol women had more freedom than most, which shows variation. The other options rely on extreme words: "identical," "ended," and "only."
why: 'Identical in every single part' is far too extreme.
The passage does not say Mongol rule ended class distinctions.
'The only patriarchal society' is false; most societies were patriarchal.

questions.stem: The information in the passage can best be used as evidence that
options: Indian Ocean states relied mainly on farming to pay for their governments.
states could grow wealthy by taxing trade that passed through their ports.
European states controlled Indian Ocean commerce through their own customs systems.
Gujarat's wealth depended on the protection of Mongol armies on land.
questions.exp: Gujarat raised enormous revenue from customs and port fees, showing that states could grow wealthy by taxing trade. The passage does not say Indian Ocean states relied on farming, that European states controlled the trade, or that Mongol armies protected Gujarat.
why: The passage describes revenue from customs and port fees, not farming.
No European control of Indian Ocean commerce is mentioned.
Gujarat's wealth came from port customs, not from Mongol armies.

questions.stem: Gujarat's economic role was most similar to that of which of the following?
options: Kashgar, whose river valley grew the food that travelers needed.
Timbuktu, whose scholars wrote and sold books in the 1500s.
Malacca, which collected fees from ships on a crucial route.
Hangzhou, a cultural center that was home to famous poets.
questions.exp: Both Gujarat and Malacca grew wealthy as go-betweens that taxed or charged fees on trade. The other cities are best known for food supply, learning, or culture.
why: Kashgar is known for food supply from its river valley, not for charging fees on trade.
Timbuktu is known for learning and books in the 1500s, not for taxing a strait.
Hangzhou is known as a cultural center, not for collecting fees as a go-between.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: Islamic scholars brought back mathematics texts from India.
Greek scholars translated Arabic works into Latin.
Paper was invented by Islamic scholars in Baghdad.
Aristotle's works were lost before they could be translated.
questions.exp: The paragraph says scholars brought back mathematics texts from India and papermaking techniques from China. It says Islamic scholars translated Greek works into Arabic (not the reverse) and saved Aristotle's works, and it says papermaking came from China.
why: Islamic scholars translated Greek works into Arabic, not Arabic works into Latin.
Paper came from China, not from Islamic scholars in Baghdad.
Islamic scholars saved Aristotle's works instead of losing them.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a claim made in the second paragraph?
options: Papermaking arrived in Europe before it reached the Islamic world.
Printing technology began in Europe and later spread to China.
Rising literacy in Europe led directly to the spread of papermaking.
Papermaking and printing helped lead to rising literacy in Europe.
questions.exp: The paragraph says papermaking reached Europe from China in the 13th century and, with printing, helped lead to a rise in literacy. It does not say papermaking reached Europe first, that printing began in Europe, or that literacy caused papermaking.
why: Papermaking reached the Islamic world before it reached Europe.
The paragraph says printing began in China, not Europe.
The paragraph reverses cause and effect; papermaking helped raise literacy, not the other way around.

sections.name: SAQs
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term, date, or detail from the source or your knowledge), A = Analysis (explain how that evidence proves your topic sentence, using "which led to," "because," or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B, and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
Each part is worth 1 point. Name a specific, accurate piece of evidence (a person, place, term, date, or technology), then explain how it connects to what the question asks.
"Describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why, using a link such as "which led to," "because," or "this allowed."
Stay inside 1200 to 1450 unless the question says otherwise.
Sentence frame: "One way ___ was ___. For example, ___. This mattered because ___."
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ on the real test: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.

Self-check before you reveal the answer: Did I give a specific example, not just a general idea? Did I explain the connection? Is it the right time and place? Did I answer the exact verb (describe or explain)?

SQ1.title: Matthew Paris on the Mongols, 1240
SQ1.attr: Matthew Paris, an English Benedictine monk writing from an abbey in England, Chronica Majora, 1240.
SQ1.text: Swarming like locusts over the face of the earth, they [the Mongols] have brought terrible devastation to the eastern parts [of Europe], laying it waste with fire and carnage. After having passed through the land of the Saracens [Muslims], they have razed cities, cut down forests, overthrown fortresses, pulled up vines, destroyed gardens, killed townspeople and peasants.

SQ2.title: Marco Polo on Hangzhou

SQ2.text: They use paper money as currency. The men as well as the women are fair-skinned and handsome. Most of them always dress themselves in silk, as a result of the vast quantities of that material produced in Hangzhou, exclusive of what the merchants import from other provinces.

At its height his fleet included more than 300 ships carrying about 28,000 people. The voyages displayed the might of the Ming Dynasty and brought tribute from the peoples Zheng He met. Some officials, however, thought the voyages were too costly, and the voyages ended in 1433.

SQ5.label: Practice source (adapted for practice).
