parts.prompt: Describe one claim Matthew Paris makes about the Mongols.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: One claim Matthew Paris makes is that the Mongols caused terrible destruction in eastern Europe. He writes that they "razed cities, cut down forests, overthrown fortresses" and "killed townspeople and peasants." This shows he portrays the Mongols as a destructive invading force that attacked civilians as well as armies.
tea: One claim Matthew Paris makes is that the Mongols caused terrible destruction in eastern Europe.
He writes that they "razed cities, cut down forests, overthrown fortresses" and "killed townspeople and peasants."
This shows he portrays the Mongols as a destructive invading force that attacked civilians as well as armies.
parts.earns: You accurately describe any specific claim in the passage (for example, that the Mongols razed cities, killed civilians, destroyed farmland, or passed through Muslim lands before reaching Europe).
parts.weak: "He says the Mongols were bad." This does not name a specific claim from the text.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that Mongol rule, despite the violence described in the excerpt, helped expand networks of exchange between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way Mongol rule expanded networks of exchange was by making Silk Roads travel safer, a period known as the Pax Mongolica. The Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and ran the yam, a relay system of posts with fresh horses and supplies. With less risk of robbery and faster, safer travel, merchants could carry goods farther across Eurasia, which increased trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
tea: One way Mongol rule expanded networks of exchange was by making Silk Roads travel safer, a period known as the Pax Mongolica.
The Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and ran the yam, a relay system of posts with fresh horses and supplies.
With less risk of robbery and faster, safer travel, merchants could carry goods farther across Eurasia, which increased trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
parts.earns: You name a specific Mongol policy or condition (Pax Mongolica, safer roads, punished banditry, the yam relay, one authority that respected merchants, religious tolerance) and explain how it increased trade.
parts.weak: "The Mongols helped trade a lot." (No specific evidence and no explanation.) Also avoid saying the Mongols created the Silk Roads; the routes already existed.

parts.prompt: Explain one cultural, technological, or environmental effect of the increased connections that Mongol rule created.
parts.skill: Explaining an effect with specific evidence
parts.model: One effect of the connections Mongol rule created was the spread of the bubonic plague. The Black Death traveled along trade routes from Central Asia and reached Europe by 1347, killing roughly a third of Europe's people. Because Mongol-linked routes moved people and goods quickly over huge distances, they also moved disease, and the resulting labor shortages in Europe raised wages.
tea: One effect of the connections Mongol rule created was the spread of the bubonic plague.
The Black Death traveled along trade routes from Central Asia and reached Europe by 1347, killing roughly a third of Europe's people.
Because Mongol-linked routes moved people and goods quickly over huge distances, they also moved disease, and the resulting labor shortages in Europe raised wages.
parts.earns: You give one specific effect (a technology, body of knowledge, religion, crop, or disease) and explain how the connections caused it.
parts.weak: "Ideas and diseases spread." This names no specific example and does not explain the link.

parts.prompt: Describe one piece of evidence in the excerpt that shows Hangzhou was part of a commercial economy.
parts.skill: Describing evidence from a source
parts.model: Polo's description shows that Hangzhou had a commercial economy. He says people "use paper money as currency" and that Hangzhou produced vast quantities of silk while merchants also imported goods from other provinces. Paper money, silk made in large amounts for sale, and imports from other provinces show goods were bought and sold across a large market, not just made for local use.
tea: Polo's description shows that Hangzhou had a commercial economy.
He says people "use paper money as currency" and that Hangzhou produced vast quantities of silk while merchants also imported goods from other provinces.
Paper money, silk made in large amounts for sale, and imports from other provinces show goods were bought and sold across a large market, not just made for local use.
parts.earns: You accurately describe any trade-related detail from the passage (paper money, large-scale silk production, or merchants importing goods).
parts.weak: "Polo says it was a nice city." This is not evidence of commerce.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that commercial innovations such as the one Polo mentions helped long-distance trade grow between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way paper money helped long-distance trade grow was by making large payments easier to carry and trust. Chinese flying cash and paper money let a merchant deposit money in one city and withdraw it in another, and bills of exchange worked in a similar way. Merchants no longer had to haul heavy copper coins over dangerous routes, so they could make larger deals over longer distances, which increased trade along the Silk Roads.
tea: One way paper money helped long-distance trade grow was by making large payments easier to carry and trust.
Chinese flying cash and paper money let a merchant deposit money in one city and withdraw it in another, and bills of exchange worked in a similar way.
Merchants no longer had to haul heavy copper coins over dangerous routes, so they could make larger deals over longer distances, which increased trade along the Silk Roads.
parts.earns: You name a specific innovation (flying cash, paper money, bills of exchange, banking houses) and explain how it made long-distance trade easier or safer.
parts.weak: "Money made trade easier." This does not name a specific innovation or explain how it helped. Also remember these credit tools were existing technologies that were improved and spread, not brand-new inventions of 1200.

parts.prompt: Explain one way Marco Polo's point of view limits this excerpt as evidence about Chinese society.
parts.skill: Sourcing and point of view
parts.model: Polo's point of view limits this excerpt because he was a foreign merchant writing for Europeans. Polo was a Venetian merchant who visited the court of Kublai Khan and wrote about China after returning to Italy in 1295. As an outsider focused on trade, he may have exaggerated or ignored parts of Chinese society that did not interest merchants, so historians must check his account against Chinese sources.
tea: Polo's point of view limits this excerpt because he was a foreign merchant writing for Europeans.
Polo was a Venetian merchant who visited the court of Kublai Khan and wrote about China after returning to Italy in 1295.
As an outsider focused on trade, he may have exaggerated or ignored parts of Chinese society that did not interest merchants, so historians must check his account against Chinese sources.
parts.earns: You identify something specific about Polo (a merchant, a Venetian, an outsider, writing for Europeans) and explain how it could limit what the source shows.
parts.weak: "He might be biased." This does not explain why or how his point of view matters.

parts.prompt: Describe one pattern shown in the table.
parts.skill: Describing a pattern in a source
parts.model: One pattern in the table is that goods moved in both directions, with each region sending what the other lacked. Gold, ivory, and enslaved people went north across the Sahara, while salt, horses, and books went south. This shows trans-Saharan trade was a two-way exchange built on the different resources of North Africa and West Africa.
tea: One pattern in the table is that goods moved in both directions, with each region sending what the other lacked.
Gold, ivory, and enslaved people went north across the Sahara, while salt, horses, and books went south.
This shows trans-Saharan trade was a two-way exchange built on the different resources of North Africa and West Africa.
parts.earns: You accurately describe a pattern in the data (two-way exchange, salt traded for gold, or different regions supplying different goods).
parts.weak: "There were many goods." This is not a pattern from the table.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that technology or the environment shaped trans-Saharan trade between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way technology shaped trans-Saharan trade was the camel saddle. Saddles developed by the Somalis let camels carry loads of up to about 600 pounds, and camels could travel long distances with little water. This let large caravans move heavy goods such as salt from oasis to oasis across the desert, which made regular long-distance trade possible.
tea: One way technology shaped trans-Saharan trade was the camel saddle.
Saddles developed by the Somalis let camels carry loads of up to about 600 pounds, and camels could travel long distances with little water.
This let large caravans move heavy goods such as salt from oasis to oasis across the desert, which made regular long-distance trade possible.
parts.earns: You name a specific factor (the camel saddle, camels, caravans, or oases) and explain how it made desert trade possible or bigger.
parts.weak: "Camels helped." This does not explain how. Also avoid saying the saddle started the trade; it improved an existing trade.

parts.prompt: Explain one effect of the growth of trans-Saharan trade on West African societies between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining an effect with specific evidence
parts.model: One effect of trans-Saharan trade was that it made the Mali Empire wealthy and strengthened Islam in West Africa. Mali's rulers taxed and protected the gold trade, and after Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca displayed this wealth, he built mosques and schools in Timbuktu. Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning, which spread Islam and increased the prestige and power of Mali's rulers.
tea: One effect of trans-Saharan trade was that it made the Mali Empire wealthy and strengthened Islam in West Africa.
Mali's rulers taxed and protected the gold trade, and after Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca displayed this wealth, he built mosques and schools in Timbuktu.
Timbuktu became a center of Islamic learning, which spread Islam and increased the prestige and power of Mali's rulers.
parts.earns: You give one specific effect (Mali's rise and wealth, Mansa Musa, Timbuktu, or the spread of Islam through merchants) and connect it to the growth of trade.
parts.weak: "Mali got rich." This does not explain how trade caused it or give specific evidence.

parts.prompt: Describe one purpose of Zheng He's voyages, according to the excerpt.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: One purpose of Zheng He's voyages was to show the power of the Ming Dynasty. The excerpt says the voyages "displayed the might of the Ming Dynasty" and brought tribute from the peoples Zheng He met. Sending more than 300 ships carrying about 28,000 people showed foreign rulers China's strength and gained tribute for the emperor.
tea: One purpose of Zheng He's voyages was to show the power of the Ming Dynasty.
The excerpt says the voyages "displayed the might of the Ming Dynasty" and brought tribute from the peoples Zheng He met.
Sending more than 300 ships carrying about 28,000 people showed foreign rulers China's strength and gained tribute for the emperor.
parts.earns: You name a purpose stated in the passage (displaying Ming power or collecting tribute).
parts.weak: "To explore." The passage does not say this, and the question asks for a purpose according to the excerpt.

parts.prompt: Explain one way earlier developments in Indian Ocean trade made voyages like Zheng He's possible.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Earlier navigation knowledge and ship technology made voyages like Zheng He's possible. Sailors already understood the seasonal monsoon winds and used the magnetic compass, the stern rudder, and large compartmented Chinese junks, and ports such as Calicut were already established. This let the fleet time its voyages, steer across open water, and sail to existing trading ports instead of exploring from scratch.
tea: Earlier navigation knowledge and ship technology made voyages like Zheng He's possible.
Sailors already understood the seasonal monsoon winds and used the magnetic compass, the stern rudder, and large compartmented Chinese junks, and ports such as Calicut were already established.
This let the fleet time its voyages, steer across open water, and sail to existing trading ports instead of exploring from scratch.
parts.earns: You name a specific earlier development (monsoon knowledge, the compass, the astrolabe, the rudder, lateen sails, junks, or established ports) and explain how it enabled the voyages.
parts.weak: "Zheng He started trade across the ocean." This is incorrect; Indian Ocean trade was centuries old, and Zheng He's voyages built on it.

parts.prompt: Explain one reason the Ming government ended the voyages.
parts.skill: Explaining a development with specific evidence
parts.model: One reason the Ming government ended the voyages was Confucian opposition and their high cost. Confucian scholars distrusted foreign contact and trade, officials thought the fleets were too expensive, and Yongle's successor ended the voyages in 1433. Because the court valued China's stable, agrarian society over overseas expansion and thought the cost was not worth it, it stopped funding the fleets.
tea: One reason the Ming government ended the voyages was Confucian opposition and their high cost.
Confucian scholars distrusted foreign contact and trade, officials thought the fleets were too expensive, and Yongle's successor ended the voyages in 1433.
Because the court valued China's stable, agrarian society over overseas expansion and thought the cost was not worth it, it stopped funding the fleets.
parts.earns: You give a specific reason (Confucian opposition to foreign contact, the cost of the fleets, or the successor's policy against overseas sailing) and explain how it led to the end of the voyages.
parts.weak: "They didn't want to do it anymore." This gives no reason and no evidence.

parts.prompt: Describe one difference between two of the networks shown in the table.
parts.skill: Describing a difference from a source
parts.model: One difference is that the Silk Roads were an overland network while the Indian Ocean network was a sea network. The Silk Roads mostly carried luxury goods such as silk and porcelain by caravan, while Indian Ocean ships also carried bulky goods. Ships could carry far more weight than camels, so sea trade moved a wider range of products than overland trade.
tea: One difference is that the Silk Roads were an overland network while the Indian Ocean network was a sea network.
The Silk Roads mostly carried luxury goods such as silk and porcelain by caravan, while Indian Ocean ships also carried bulky goods.
Ships could carry far more weight than camels, so sea trade moved a wider range of products than overland trade.
parts.earns: You accurately describe a difference shown in the table (terrain, transport, technology, or goods) between two named networks.
parts.weak: "They were different." This does not name the networks or any specific difference.

parts.prompt: Explain one similarity between the Silk Roads and the Indian Ocean trade networks in the period 1200 to 1450.
parts.skill: Comparison with specific evidence
parts.model: One similarity is that both networks produced powerful trading cities. Samarkand grew rich on the Silk Roads, and Calicut grew rich on the Indian Ocean network. Cities where routes met earned money from taxes, markets, and services for merchants, so trade built urban wealth in both networks.
tea: One similarity is that both networks produced powerful trading cities.
Samarkand grew rich on the Silk Roads, and Calicut grew rich on the Indian Ocean network.
Cities where routes met earned money from taxes, markets, and services for merchants, so trade built urban wealth in both networks.
parts.earns: You name a specific similarity (growth built on existing routes, state protection, improved technology, trading cities, diasporic merchant communities, or the spread of religions) and support it with evidence from both networks.
parts.weak: "Both traded things." This is too general and gives no evidence from either network.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that geography shaped the technology used on one of these networks.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: One way geography shaped technology was that the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean shaped sailing technology. Seasonal monsoon winds led sailors to rely on the lateen sail, the compass, and the astrolabe. These tools let ships use the winds and navigate open water out of sight of land, which made regular ocean crossings possible. (Another strong answer: in the Sahara, scarce water made camels and load-bearing saddles essential.)
tea: One way geography shaped technology was that the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean shaped sailing technology.
Seasonal monsoon winds led sailors to rely on the lateen sail, the compass, and the astrolabe.

These tools let ships use the winds and navigate open water out of sight of land, which made regular ocean crossings possible. (Another strong answer: in the Sahara, scarce water made camels and load-bearing saddles essential.)
parts.earns: You link a specific geographic feature (monsoon winds, open sea, desert, scarce water, mountains) to a specific technology and explain why the technology fit that geography.
parts.weak: "Geography mattered a lot." This names no feature, technology, or link between them.

parts.prompt: Describe one likely audience for Margery Kempe's account of her pilgrimages.
parts.skill: Audience and purpose
parts.model: One likely audience for Kempe's account was fellow Christians interested in religious devotion and pilgrimage. She describes pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Spain and says she was so overcome by her first sight of Jerusalem that she nearly fell off her donkey. This focus on holy places and emotional devotion suggests she meant it for religious readers who valued pilgrimage and spiritual experience.
tea: One likely audience for Kempe's account was fellow Christians interested in religious devotion and pilgrimage.
She describes pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Spain and says she was so overcome by her first sight of Jerusalem that she nearly fell off her donkey.
This focus on holy places and emotional devotion suggests she meant it for religious readers who valued pilgrimage and spiritual experience.
parts.earns: You describe a plausible audience (such as Christian readers, other pilgrims, or members of her community) and tie it to the content of the account.
parts.weak: "Many people." This names no audience and does not connect to the source.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that established travel and trade routes in the period 1200 to 1450 made pilgrimages like Kempe's possible.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Established travel and trade routes made pilgrimages like Kempe's possible. By the 1400s, Mediterranean sea routes and overland routes across Europe were active, and the Crusades had increased European contact with Byzantine and Islamic lands. Pilgrims could travel on the same routes, ports, and roads that merchants used, so reaching Jerusalem and Rome was practical.
tea: Established travel and trade routes made pilgrimages like Kempe's possible.
By the 1400s, Mediterranean sea routes and overland routes across Europe were active, and the Crusades had increased European contact with Byzantine and Islamic lands.
Pilgrims could travel on the same routes, ports, and roads that merchants used, so reaching Jerusalem and Rome was practical.
parts.earns: You name a specific route or development (Mediterranean sea routes, overland routes across Europe, merchant networks, or contact increased by the Crusades) and explain how it made travel possible.
parts.weak: "Travel was easier then." This is vague and gives no specific route or development.

parts.prompt: Explain one difference between Margery Kempe's account and Marco Polo's account of his travels, based on the point of view of each author.
parts.skill: Sourcing and point of view
parts.model: One difference is that Polo's account focuses on trade while Kempe's focuses on religious experience. Polo, a Venetian merchant, described wealth and cities in China, while Kempe, a Christian pilgrim, described visions and her emotional reaction to holy places. Their different identities and purposes shaped what each author chose to notice and record.
tea: One difference is that Polo's account focuses on trade while Kempe's focuses on religious experience.
Polo, a Venetian merchant, described wealth and cities in China, while Kempe, a Christian pilgrim, described visions and her emotional reaction to holy places.
Their different identities and purposes shaped what each author chose to notice and record.
parts.earns: You identify a specific difference in focus or purpose and tie it to each author's identity (merchant versus religious pilgrim).
parts.weak: "They were different people." This does not explain how their points of view shaped their accounts.

parts.prompt: Describe one way the map shows that the Mongol Empire was divided in the 13th century.
parts.skill: Describing evidence from a map
parts.model: The map shows the Mongol Empire was divided into separate regions in the 13th century. It labels four regions: the Empire of the Great Khans/Yuan Dynasty, the Chaghatai Khanate, the Ilkhan Empire, and the Batu Kipchak Empire (Golden Horde). Because each region has its own name and shading, the map shows the empire had split into separate khanates ruled by different branches of the family.
tea: The map shows the Mongol Empire was divided into separate regions in the 13th century.
It labels four regions: the Empire of the Great Khans/Yuan Dynasty, the Chaghatai Khanate, the Ilkhan Empire, and the Batu Kipchak Empire (Golden Horde).
Because each region has its own name and shading, the map shows the empire had split into separate khanates ruled by different branches of the family.
parts.earns: You accurately describe the division using a detail visible on the map (named khanates or regions), not just the idea that it was big.
parts.weak: "The Mongols had a lot of land." This does not describe division or use a detail from the map.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that Mongol rule across the lands shown on the map affected trade on the Silk Roads in the period 1200 to 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Mongol rule over the lands on the map made Silk Roads trade safer and bigger. One ruling family controlled most of the overland route from China to the Black Sea, and the Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and protected merchants (the Pax Mongolica). With safer travel under one authority, merchants could move goods farther with less risk, increasing trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
tea: Mongol rule over the lands on the map made Silk Roads trade safer and bigger.
One ruling family controlled most of the overland route from China to the Black Sea, and the Mongols improved roads, punished bandits, and protected merchants (the Pax Mongolica).
With safer travel under one authority, merchants could move goods farther with less risk, increasing trade between East Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
parts.earns: You name a specific Mongol policy or condition (safer roads, protection of merchants, unified control of the routes, the Pax Mongolica) and explain how it increased or changed trade.
parts.weak: "The Mongols helped trade." This gives no specific action and no explanation.

parts.prompt: Explain one way the Mongol conquests shown on the map led to the spread of disease or technology between regions.
parts.skill: Explaining a development with specific evidence
parts.model: Mongol conquests spread technology between regions. Chinese technologies such as gunpowder and papermaking moved west along routes the Mongols controlled, and the bubonic plague spread the same way in the 14th century. Mongol control linked China, Southwest Asia, and Europe, so ideas, tools, and diseases traveled along the same connected routes.
tea: Mongol conquests spread technology between regions.
Chinese technologies such as gunpowder and papermaking moved west along routes the Mongols controlled, and the bubonic plague spread the same way in the 14th century.
Mongol control linked China, Southwest Asia, and Europe, so ideas, tools, and diseases traveled along the same connected routes.
parts.earns: You name a specific technology or disease (gunpowder, paper, printing, compass, bubonic plague) and explain how Mongol-linked routes carried it between regions.
parts.weak: "Things spread because the empire was big." This names no technology or disease and no mechanism.

parts.prompt: Describe one feature of the geography shown on the map that made the Strait of Malacca important to the Indian Ocean trade network.
parts.skill: Describing evidence from a map
parts.model: The Strait of Malacca mattered because it is a narrow passage linking two seas. The map shows it between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea, and the caption calls it the shortest route between East Asia and Southwest Asia. Because ships going between the two regions had to pass through it, whoever controlled the strait could profit from the trade.
tea: The Strait of Malacca mattered because it is a narrow passage linking two seas.
The map shows it between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea, and the caption calls it the shortest route between East Asia and Southwest Asia.
Because ships going between the two regions had to pass through it, whoever controlled the strait could profit from the trade.
parts.earns: You describe a geographic feature shown on the map (a narrow strait linking two seas, the shortest route between East and Southwest Asia) and tie it to trade.
parts.weak: "It was near water." This is too vague and does not use the map.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that the Indian Ocean trade network affected the development of a trading city or state in the period 1200 to 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining an effect with specific evidence
parts.model: Indian Ocean trade made the city-state of Malacca wealthy and more centralized. Malacca charged fees on the ships and cargoes passing through the strait and used that wealth to build a strong navy against pirates. Running a navy and collecting fees required centralized planning, so trade increased the power of Malacca's government.
tea: Indian Ocean trade made the city-state of Malacca wealthy and more centralized.
Malacca charged fees on the ships and cargoes passing through the strait and used that wealth to build a strong navy against pirates.
Running a navy and collecting fees required centralized planning, so trade increased the power of Malacca's government.
parts.earns: You name a specific city or state (Malacca, Gujarat, Swahili city-states such as Kilwa or Mombasa, Calicut) and explain how trade changed it (wealth, customs, centralization, growth).
parts.weak: "Trade made cities rich." This names no city and gives no explanation.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that technology or knowledge allowed merchants to sail the route shown on the map.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Sailing technology and knowledge of the winds let merchants cross the Indian Ocean. Sailors used the lateen sail, the monsoon winds, and navigation tools such as the compass and the astrolabe. These let ships sail across open water on a predictable schedule and find their way to ports such as Malacca.
tea: Sailing technology and knowledge of the winds let merchants cross the Indian Ocean.
Sailors used the lateen sail, the monsoon winds, and navigation tools such as the compass and the astrolabe.
These let ships sail across open water on a predictable schedule and find their way to ports such as Malacca.
parts.earns: You name a specific technology or knowledge (lateen sail, monsoon wind knowledge, compass, astrolabe, dhow, junk) and explain how it made the voyage possible.
parts.weak: "They had good ships." This names no technology and does not explain.

sections.name: Mock MCQs
examTips: Treat this like the real test: turn the Timer on, leave Shuffle off, and work through all 13 questions without looking anything up.
Aim for about one minute per question. Mark hard ones with Flag for review and come back.
You can check answers as you go or at the end; checking only at the end is closer to real test conditions.
When you finish, do the "Mock Test: SAQs" tab (about 13 minutes per SAQ), then use Retest Missed Questions on each tab.
tips: Read the question stem before the source so you know what you are looking for.

For "best used as evidence of" or "best illustrates" questions, first name the idea the source shows (cause, effect, continuity, change, connection between regions), then pick the option that matches that idea.
Eliminate options that are true in history but not shown by the source, or that belong to the wrong time or region.
Watch for extreme words ("only," "all," "first," "created," "ended," "every"): they are usually wrong.
For "claim" or "evidence the author uses" questions, the answer must be stated or directly supported in the text. Do not use outside knowledge to pick it.
For point-of-view questions, ask who wrote it, when, for whom, and why.

S11.title: An official argues against the treasure voyages
S11.attr: Adapted from the arguments of Ming officials who opposed the voyages.
S11.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: The treasure fleets have sailed seven times and have cost the treasury sums that could have fed provinces. They return with giraffes and rare spices, curiosities that add nothing to the strength of the empire.

The foundation of the empire is the farmer and the family. Sailors who spend years among foreign peoples learn foreign customs and forget their duties to their ancestors. The emperor's successor would do well to end these voyages and keep the people at home.

S12.title: Samarkand
S12.attr: Adapted from a textbook description of Samarkand.
S12.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S12.text: Samarkand, in the valley of the Zeravshan River, was a stopping point on the Silk Roads between China and the Mediterranean. Archaeologists have found evidence of Christianity, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, and Islam among its former residents. Between 1417 and 1422, the city's rulers built a large madrasa, a school for Islamic learning, which still stands. The city was also known for its artisans, who produced goods sold in its markets.

S13.title: The court of Kublai Khan
S13.attr: Adapted description of the court of Kublai Khan.
S13.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S13.text: Kublai Khan allows the people of his empire to follow their own religions. At his court there are Buddhist monks, Daoist priests, Muslim scholars, and Christian missionaries, and he consults them all. He gives high office to foreigners, including merchants from the western lands, because he trusts them more than he trusts the scholars of the Chinese cities.

S14.title: The setbacks of Constantinople
S14.label: Practice source (adapted for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
S14.text: Constantinople, long a great trading city, suffered a series of blows. In 1204, soldiers of the Fourth Crusade attacked and weakened it. In 1346 and again in 1349, the bubonic plague killed roughly half its people. After a siege of 53 days, the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

S15.title: Enslaved people in the Indian Ocean trade
S15.attr: Adapted summary of a textbook account.
S15.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: Merchants in East African ports sold enslaved people to buyers in northern Africa, the Middle East, and India. Many were put to work in seaports, in the shipping industry, and as household servants, and some served as sailors or soldiers.

Because they lived in towns and cities, enslaved people had more chances to form communities and to work alongside free laborers than those later taken to the Americas. African words, musical styles, and customs can still be found in Oman, India, and elsewhere.

questions.stem: The author describes the giraffes and rare spices as 'curiosities' most likely in order to
options: summarize accurately why the emperor had ordered the voyages.
argue that the voyages gave little benefit for their cost.
praise the fleets for bringing wonders from distant lands.
give the treasury a neutral list of what the fleets brought.
questions.exp: The author lists the giraffes and spices to argue that the voyages cost a great deal and added nothing to the empire's strength. The word choice is persuasive criticism, not a summary of the emperor's goals, praise, or a neutral list.
why: The author is arguing against the voyages, not summarizing the emperor's goals.
Calling the items 'curiosities' belittles them; it is not praise.
The word choice is persuasive, not a neutral list.

questions.stem: The author's argument most clearly reflects which of the following?
options: Confucian concern that foreign contact would weaken a stable, agrarian society.
Muslim merchants' wish to take a larger share of Indian Ocean trade and port revenue.
Mongol officials' fear of growing Ming naval power in Southeast Asia.
Buddhist monks' opposition to government-sponsored overseas travel.
questions.exp: The author stresses that the empire rests on the farmer and the family and warns that sailors forget their duties to their ancestors, which reflects the Confucian emphasis on a stable agrarian social order. The passage has no Muslim merchant, Mongol, or Buddhist perspective.
why: No Muslim merchant perspective or interest in port revenue appears in the passage.
No Mongol officials or fear of Ming naval power are mentioned.
No Buddhist monks or opposition on religious grounds appear in the passage.

questions.stem: The view expressed in the passage differs most sharply from which of the following?
options: The Confucian view that farming is the base of a stable and orderly society.
The later ban on building ships with more than two masts.
The emperor's use of the fleets to show power and collect tribute.
The successor's decision to end the voyages after Yongle's reign.
questions.exp: The author wants the voyages ended and the people kept at home, which clashes with the emperor's use of the fleets to show power and collect tribute abroad. The emphasis on farming, the ban on larger ships, and the successor's decision to end the voyages all fit the author's view.
why: The Confucian view that farming is the base of society agrees with the author.
The ban on large ships fits the author's wish to limit sea travel.
The successor ending the voyages agrees with the author's view.

questions.stem: The religious evidence described in the passage best illustrates which of the following about trade cities in this period?
options: They were governed by religious leaders who enforced a single faith.
They declined once merchants carried new religions to distant regions.
They relied on state-sponsored conversion programs to attract foreign merchants and scholars.
They were crossroads where merchants and travelers from different cultures met.
questions.exp: Evidence of Christianity, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, and Islam shows people of many faiths living in a Silk Road city. Nothing suggests a single enforced faith, decline caused by the spread of religions, or state-run conversion.
why: The evidence of many faiths shows tolerance, not a single enforced faith.
Nothing says cities declined because religions spread.
State-run conversion programs are not mentioned.

questions.stem: The construction of the madrasa between 1417 and 1422 is best used as evidence that
options: Islamic scholarship in Central Asia ended after the Mongol conquests.
wealth from trade helped support centers of learning in major cities.
Samarkand's rulers had turned away from the Silk Roads toward farming.
the Ming government paid for religious schools across Central Asia.
questions.exp: A major madrasa in a Silk Road city shows that trade cities also became centers of learning supported by their wealth. Islamic scholarship continued under Turkic rulers, and nothing connects the Ming or farming to the madrasa.
why: The madrasa was built after the Mongol conquests, so scholarship did not end.
A major madrasa shows investment in learning, not a turn away from the Silk Roads.
The Ming government is not connected to the madrasa.

questions.stem: Samarkand's role in Silk Roads trade is most similar to which role played by Timbuktu in trans-Saharan trade?
options: A coastal port that collected fees from ships using a narrow strait.
A desert oasis that supplied salt to the caravans crossing the Sahara.
A trading city that also became a center of Islamic learning.
A capital that controlled the mines producing the region's gold.
questions.exp: Both were trading cities that also became centers of Islamic learning. The coastal strait fits Malacca, the salt oasis fits Taghaza, and Timbuktu was a city of trade and learning rather than a mining center.
why: A coastal port collecting strait fees describes Malacca, not Timbuktu.
A salt-supplying oasis describes Taghaza, not Timbuktu.
Timbuktu was a trade and learning city, not a gold-mining center.

questions.stem: The religious policy described in the passage most closely continued the policy of which earlier Mongol ruler?
options: Genghis Khan, who allowed many religions within his empire.
Hulegu, who destroyed Baghdad and killed the caliph.
Batu, who made Russian princes convert as the price of tribute.
Timur, who spread Islam by force across Central Asia.
questions.exp: Genghis Khan instituted religious tolerance throughout the empire, and Kublai Khan, like his grandfather, tolerated many faiths. Hulegu's destruction of Baghdad was not a religious policy, and Batu and Timur (who came later) did not act as the other options describe.
why: Hulegu's destruction of Baghdad was not a religious policy of tolerance.
Batu did not require Russian princes to convert as the price of tribute.
Timur came later and did not follow a policy of tolerance.

questions.stem: To judge how reliably the passage reflects Kublai Khan's actual policy, a historian would most need to know
options: how many religions were practiced in China before the Mongol conquests.
whether the Mongols used the yam relay system to carry messages.
which Mongol ruler first adopted the Uyghur script for Mongol.
who wrote the passage and whether the writer saw the court firsthand.
questions.exp: To judge reliability, a historian needs to know who wrote the passage and whether the writer saw the court firsthand. The other facts are true or interesting but do not bear on whether this account is reliable.
why: Religions in China before the Mongols do not show whether this account is reliable.
The yam relay system has nothing to do with the passage's reliability.
Which ruler adopted the Uyghur script does not bear on the source's reliability.

questions.stem: The passage best supports which of the following causal arguments?
options: Hiring foreigners made Chinese scholars more loyal to Mongol rule.
Religious tolerance at court brought people of many faiths into service.
Consulting religious leaders let Kublai rule without relying on military force.
The Mongols' trust in merchants turned their empire into a Buddhist state.
questions.exp: Monks, priests, scholars, and missionaries all at court, plus foreigners holding office, support the argument that tolerance brought people of many faiths into service. The passage says Kublai trusted foreigners more than Chinese scholars, so it does not support greater scholar loyalty, avoiding force, or a Buddhist state.
why: The passage says Kublai trusted foreigners more than Chinese scholars, so it does not support greater scholar loyalty.
Nothing suggests consulting religious leaders let him avoid military force.
The passage does not claim a Buddhist state resulted from trust in merchants.

questions.stem: The history of Constantinople described in the passage can best be used as evidence that
options: disease struck only the cities of Europe and the Mediterranean.
political stability alone was enough to protect a trading city's wealth.
the prosperity of trading cities was neither guaranteed nor permanent.
the Ottoman conquest ended all trade between Europe and Asia.
questions.exp: Invasion, plague, and conquest steadily weakened Constantinople, showing that a trading city's prosperity could disappear. The plague struck cities across Eurasia, and the passage does not say the Ottoman conquest ended all trade.
why: The plague struck cities across Eurasia, not only Europe and the Mediterranean.
'Alone was enough' is too strong; the passage shows stable states still lost wealth.
The passage does not say Ottoman conquest ended all trade between Europe and Asia.

questions.stem: Which of the following cities experienced a decline most similar in cause to Constantinople's setbacks from invasion?
options: Kashgar, which declined after invasion and Tamerlane's attack.
Hangzhou, which grew as the southern end of the Grand Canal in China.
Malacca, which grew rich from fees on ships using the busy strait.
Timbuktu, which became a famous center of trade and Islamic learning.
questions.exp: Kashgar declined after conquests by nomadic invaders and was ravaged by Tamerlane in 1389–90. The other cities are examples of growth through trade.
why: Hangzhou grew through trade, so it is not an example of decline.
Malacca grew rich from fees, which is not a decline.
Timbuktu grew as a center of trade and learning, which is not a decline.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in the first paragraph?
options: Most enslaved people were sent to farms in southern India.
Enslaved people were sold only to buyers within East Africa.
Merchants in northern Africa bought most enslaved people from India.
Some enslaved people worked as sailors or soldiers in the region.
questions.exp: The first paragraph says some enslaved people served as sailors or soldiers. It says they were sold to buyers in northern Africa, the Middle East, and India, not only within East Africa, and it names seaports and households, not farms, as common workplaces.
why: The paragraph names seaports and households as workplaces, not farms in southern India.
They were sold to buyers in northern Africa, the Middle East, and India, not only within East Africa.
The first paragraph does not say merchants in northern Africa bought most enslaved people from India.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a claim made in the second paragraph?
options: Enslaved people lived under the same conditions as those taken to the Americas.
Town life gave enslaved people more chances to form communities and work with free laborers.
Enslaved people were forbidden to form communities in the cities where they lived.
African customs and music disappeared soon after enslaved people arrived in Oman and in India.
questions.exp: The paragraph says living in towns and cities gave enslaved people more chances to form communities and to work alongside free laborers than those taken to the Americas. It also says African words, music, and customs survived, so the other options contradict it.
why: The paragraph says conditions differed from those of people taken to the Americas.
The paragraph says town life gave more chances to form communities, not that they were forbidden.
The paragraph says African words, music, and customs survived.

sections.name: Mock SAQs
examTips: Turn the Timer on and give yourself about 13 minutes per SAQ (1 to plan and 12 to write).
Write complete sentences for A, B, and C, and only then click Check Answer.
tips: Use TEA for every part: T = Topic sentence (answer the question directly, restating its words), E = Evidence (a specific person, place, term, date, or detail from the source or your knowledge), A = Analysis (explain how that evidence proves your topic sentence, using "which led to," "because," or "this allowed").
Label your answers A, B, and C and write in complete sentences. No introduction or thesis.
Each part is worth 1 point. Name a specific, accurate piece of evidence (a person, place, term, date, or technology), then explain how it connects to what the question asks.
"Describe" means give accurate details. "Explain" means show how or why, using a link such as "which led to," "because," or "this allowed."
Stay inside 1200 to 1450 unless the question says otherwise.
Sentence frame: "One way ___ was ___. For example, ___. This mattered because ___."
Aim for about 13 minutes per SAQ on the real test: about 1 to plan and 12 to write.

Self-check before you reveal the answer: Did I give a specific example, not just a general idea? Did I explain the connection? Is it the right time and place? Did I answer the exact verb (describe or explain)?

MS1.title: The Sultanate of Malacca
MS1.attr: Adapted summary of a textbook account.
MS1.label: Practice source (written for practice; not a verbatim quotation).
MS1.text: The Sultanate of Malacca, a Muslim city-state on the Strait of Malacca, grew wealthy by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China. Its sultans built a navy to keep the waters safe from pirates, and in the 1400s the state expanded into Sumatra and the southern Malay Peninsula. Merchants from Arabia, India, China, and Southeast Asia lived and traded in the city until the Portuguese conquered it in 1511.

MS2.title: Why cities grew and declined
MS2.label: Practice source (adapted for practice).
table: Factors contributing to the growth of cities
Factors contributing to the decline of cities
Political stability and decline of invasions

parts.prompt: Describe one way Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth, according to the excerpt.
parts.skill: Describing a claim from a source
parts.model: Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth by charging fees on passing ships. The excerpt says the sultanate grew wealthy "by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China." Because ships traveling between India and China had to pass through the strait, the fees created a steady stream of income.
tea: Malacca's rulers used the city's location to gain wealth by charging fees on passing ships.
The excerpt says the sultanate grew wealthy "by charging fees on the ships that passed through the strait between India and China."
Because ships traveling between India and China had to pass through the strait, the fees created a steady stream of income.
parts.earns: You accurately describe a way stated in the passage (fees on passing ships, or building a navy to keep the strait safe so trade would continue).
parts.weak: "They traded a lot." This does not describe how the location produced wealth.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that knowledge of the monsoon winds contributed to the growth of trading cities such as Malacca between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Knowledge of the monsoon winds helped trading cities grow by forcing merchants to stop and wait in port. Winter winds blew from the northeast and summer winds from the southwest, so merchants had to wait in cities such as Malacca for the winds to change. Waiting merchants bought, sold, and paid fees, so the city's population and wealth grew.
tea: Knowledge of the monsoon winds helped trading cities grow by forcing merchants to stop and wait in port.
Winter winds blew from the northeast and summer winds from the southwest, so merchants had to wait in cities such as Malacca for the winds to change.
Waiting merchants bought, sold, and paid fees, so the city's population and wealth grew.
parts.earns: You link monsoon timing to a specific consequence for trading cities (merchants waiting in port, ports becoming meeting points, more trade and wealth).
parts.weak: "The wind helped them sail." This does not explain how the winds helped cities grow.

parts.prompt: Explain one way diasporic merchant communities affected the cultures of Indian Ocean port cities.
parts.skill: Explaining an effect with specific evidence
parts.model: Diasporic merchant communities blended cultures in Indian Ocean port cities. Arab and Persian merchants settled in ports such as those on the Swahili coast and in western India, married local women, and introduced Islam and the Arabic language. Local cultures also influenced the merchants, producing blended cultures such as Swahili language and culture.
tea: Diasporic merchant communities blended cultures in Indian Ocean port cities.
Arab and Persian merchants settled in ports such as those on the Swahili coast and in western India, married local women, and introduced Islam and the Arabic language.
Local cultures also influenced the merchants, producing blended cultures such as Swahili language and culture.
parts.earns: You name a specific community or place and a specific cultural effect (the spread of Islam, a blended language, intermarriage, or two-way influence).
parts.weak: "Different people lived together." This names no specific community or effect.

parts.prompt: Describe one pattern shown in the table.
parts.skill: Describing a pattern in a source
parts.model: One pattern in the table is that the factors behind a city's growth are the opposite of the factors behind its decline. Growth is linked to political stability and strong farm output, while decline is linked to instability, invasions, and falling agricultural productivity. This shows a city's fortunes depended on political security and its food supply as well as on trade.
tea: One pattern in the table is that the factors behind a city's growth are the opposite of the factors behind its decline.
Growth is linked to political stability and strong farm output, while decline is linked to instability, invasions, and falling agricultural productivity.
This shows a city's fortunes depended on political security and its food supply as well as on trade.
parts.earns: You accurately describe a pattern in the table (growth and decline factors mirror each other, or stability, commerce, and farming matter in both lists).
parts.weak: "There are many factors." This is not a pattern from the table.

parts.prompt: Explain one way that trade networks contributed to the growth of a specific city between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Trade networks made Timbuktu grow. Mali's rulers taxed and protected the trans-Saharan gold trade, and Mansa Musa built mosques and schools there. The wealth and Islamic learning drew merchants and scholars, which made Timbuktu a major center of trade and learning. (Other strong answers: Samarkand, Kashgar, Hangzhou, Malacca.)
tea: Trade networks made Timbuktu grow.
Mali's rulers taxed and protected the trans-Saharan gold trade, and Mansa Musa built mosques and schools there.
The wealth and Islamic learning drew merchants and scholars, which made Timbuktu a major center of trade and learning. (Other strong answers: Samarkand, Kashgar, Hangzhou, Malacca.)
parts.earns: You name a specific city and explain how a trade network caused its growth.
parts.weak: "Trade made cities bigger." This names no city and gives no specific link.

parts.prompt: Explain one reason a specific trading city declined between 1200 and 1450.
parts.skill: Explaining a cause with specific evidence
parts.model: Baghdad declined because of foreign invasion. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed many of its residents. The destruction of the city and its people ended its role as a major political and trading center. (Other strong answers: Constantinople after 1204 and plague; Kashgar after Tamerlane's attacks.)
tea: Baghdad declined because of foreign invasion.
The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed many of its residents.
The destruction of the city and its people ended its role as a major political and trading center. (Other strong answers: Constantinople after 1204 and plague; Kashgar after Tamerlane's attacks.)
parts.earns: You name a specific city and give a specific cause of its decline (invasion, plague, or political instability) with evidence.
parts.weak: "Cities declined because of problems." This names no city or cause.
